subject: science
passage: When a rat runs a maze, particular neurons in its hippocampus fire in a sequence that tracks its route. During the deep sleep that follows, the same sequences often fire again, compressed into a fraction of a second. Neuroscientist Kwabena Mensah argues that this "replay" is how the day's experiences are consolidated into lasting memories, and he regards it as the main reason that sleep is indispensable to learning.
passage_b: Replay is not confined to sleep. Rats pausing at the end of a maze run, fully awake, also fire compressed sequences of these neurons, sometimes tracing routes they have just taken and sometimes routes they have yet to try. Replay may well support memory, but if it occurs during quiet waking as well as during sleep, it cannot by itself explain why sleep in particular is so important for learning.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view held by Mensah in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the idea that replay plays any part in the formation of lasting memories
choices.B: By questioning whether the sequences seen during sleep truly match the rat's earlier route
choices.C: By agreeing that sleep is indispensable to learning because replay occurs only during sleep
choices.D: By allowing that replay may aid memory while doubting it explains sleep's special role

explanation.why: Text 2 says "Replay may well support memory," so it does not reject Mensah's view of what replay does. But because replay also happens "during quiet waking," Text 2 says it "cannot by itself explain why sleep in particular is so important." Text 2 accepts one part of Mensah's view and rejects the other.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says replay "may well support memory," so it does not deny replay any role.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions that sleep sequences match the earlier route.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2's main point is that replay does not occur only during sleep.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 allows that replay may help memory but argues that, since it also occurs while rats are awake, it cannot explain why sleep matters so much.
